title: What not to put on the site for a nonprofit
metaTitle: What to cut from a nonprofit website
excerpt: Cut the sad hero, the unsupported impact claims, and the pages that only perform scale. Keep the work in the world and a clear way to give, join, or read.
alt: A pale room with an arched opening onto a dark sofa, a low table, and a glass vase of dried stems, for a piece on leaving a site quieter and more specific.
caption: A quiet room with one clear opening. A shorter site can feel like this. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should come off a nonprofit homepage first?
faqs.answer: A sad photograph paired with a donate button and no program. Replace it with the work, or with a plain sentence if the right picture does not exist yet. Stock distress and autoplaying montages belong in the same cut. The visitor needs to understand before they are asked to feel.

faqs.question: Which impact claims should be deleted?
faqs.answer: Any figure you cannot point to in a report, and any quote you wrote yourself. Small, defined numbers are safer than rounded epics. Badges and partner logos stay only with a year, a scope, and a duty you would let that partner see this week.

faqs.question: How small can the site be?
faqs.answer: As small as the real offer. Programs, a way to join, a way to give, a few proofs, an about page, the report, and contact. Campaign microsites should fold back into that set when the season ends. A short site you can keep true beats a long one that performs compassion.

markdown:
The nonprofit website mistakes that push people away are often the ones the team finds moving. A sad photograph and a donate button, with no program in view, reassures staff that the site feels urgent. It confuses a donor or a participant who is trying to decide whether the work is real. Keep the work in the world. Keep a clear way to give, join, or read the program. A shorter site that tells the truth will do more than a long one that performs compassion.

Use this as a cutting list. Remove what fails the visitor, including pieces that won praise in a board meeting. The room you free is where the program, the boundary, and the next step can sit in the first screen.

## The sad photograph and the lone donate button

Start with the hero. A close crop of distress, a stock child, a dim room, and a single button that says donate. The visitor who needed the service cannot tell whether you offer it. The visitor who might fund it cannot tell what they would be funding. Both have been asked to feel instead of to understand. Replace the frame with the work, or remove the image until you have the work. Put the program sentence in the opening. Offer give, join, and read as the paths that are real, with one of them primary.

The same mistake appears in language. Lives changed. Impact delivered. Together we rise. If you delete these lines and nothing specific remains, the page was a mood. Put back the place, the hours, the person served, and the boundary. Keep a sentence about need only when it is concrete. A wait list with a number you can define. A neighborhood without this service. A cost you can show in the report. Need stated as fact. Not need staged as a hook.

Video that autoplays the sad cut is the mistake with sound. It delays the program, it startles a person in a public place, and it is worse with motion on. Use a still of the work. If a short film exists and it shows the program with consent, place it on a proof page, with a still as the poster, and keep the action visible beside it. The homepage does not owe anyone a premiere.

## Impact language with no program attached

Large numbers with no method. "Thousands served" when the sheet says something narrower, or when nobody can find the sheet. Percentages of funds to programs that you would not walk through with a donor. Composite quotes from unnamed people. They borrow the costume of evidence.

Print a number only when the report, the board packet, or the public filing will back it up, and link that source. Define the unit in the sentence. If the honest number is small because the program is small, print the small number. A precise small fact is more trustworthy than a rounded epic. Organizations that inflate are sorting themselves out of the consideration set of the donors they most want.

Awards, ratings, and seals belong only with a scope and a year, next to the program they concern. A badge row in the header, unexplained, is a trophy case. Participants do not join a trophy case. Donors who do are not the ones who will stay for the work. If a rating system requires you to contort the budget, do not build the homepage around the rating. Explain the budget in your own words and let the rating be a footnote if you keep it at all.

Partner and funder logos that are out of date, or that imply a closer role than you have, should come down. A logo is a claim. Old claims are how a careful reader loses faith in the current ones. Keep the marks you would be willing to have the partner see on the page this week, and write the duty next to any mark that changes what a participant should expect.

## Pages that perform scale

A blog that posts gala photos and reprinted press releases, and never answers a participant's question. A separate microsite for every campaign, with a new logo and no path back to the program. An events calendar whose only entry is last season. Thin "issue" pages that repeat one service under five cause headlines. These pages make a small team look large and unreliable.

Keep the pages that have jobs. Programs, the way to join, the way to give, one or two proofs, about, the report, contact. Add a page when a season truly needs it, and retire it when the season ends. Redirect the campaign URL to the program or to the report. A single site with a stable name is easier to trust than a constellation of landing pages nobody maintains.

Duplicate appeals are part of this list. The homepage, a "why give" page, and a popup that all repeat the same cry. Choose one place for the appeal and let it be specific. Repetition feels like commitment inside the organization. Outside, it feels like you do not have a second fact. [Google's helpful-content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks for a clear purpose and for pages that help a person accomplish a real task. Your purpose is the program and the honest door into it. Pages that exist to multiply slogans work against that purpose.

Footers stuffed with every social post, a shop of branded mugs that distracts from the program, and a newsletter wall before the hours are the small versions of the same error. Link the social account. Sell the mug if you must, off the main path. Ask for the email after someone has what they came for.

## Interruptions

A modal that demands an email, a gift, or a survey before the program is visible. A chat bot that covers the apply button on a phone. A cookie wall that never returns the screen to the heading. An autoplaying carousel of causes. Each of these inserts the organization's anxiety in front of the visitor's task.

Remove the modal. If a banner must exist for consent, make it one line and do not let it permanently displace the program. Remove the bot unless a person is truly behind it during the hours you claim, and unless it can say the hours and the boundary correctly. Most bots cannot. The contact path you already wrote is the conversation.

Stop the carousel. If you have several programs, list them in text under the primary one, with their status. Text stays still while someone decides whether they are in the right place. Motion that exists to feel alive is a tax. Hanabi's standard, clarity over complexity, applies directly. If the movement does not help someone see the work or take the next step, cut it. People who prefer reduced motion should never be left with a blank hero where the program used to be.

Urgent bars that stay up for months train everyone to ignore urgency. Use a bar for a real closure, a real opening, a real date. Take it down when the date passes. A site that is always on fire is a site that cannot be read.

## Navigation and forms that hide the work

A menu of internal departments. A header with no path to apply or give. Labels like "get involved" and "resources" that open junk drawers. A donate button that is the only specific word on the site. These are structural versions of the sad hero. They center the organization and hope the visitor will adapt.

Rebuild the bar around jobs. Programs, join, give, report, about, contact. Use the words the front desk uses. On a phone, keep the primary action outside the collapsed menu. Match each label to the heading it opens. Retire empty items left by a template. A calendar, a shop, a forum, a members area with nothing behind it is a door that makes you look unfinished.

Forms that ask for a life story before a person can ask a question belong on the list. Shorten them by intent. Help, volunteer, odd gift, concern. Publish the window you keep. Repeat the hours and the address in text so nobody has to write you to learn them. A ten-field form on top of a vague homepage is two mistakes compounding. Fix the homepage, then the form will have less to compensate for.

## Language that blurs the boundary

"Everyone is welcome" when the program has eligibility. "We meet you where you are" when you have one site and set hours. "We do it all" when you refer half the calls elsewhere. These sentences are meant as kindness. They function as surprises later, and surprises are how trust breaks at intake. Publish the boundary. Who, where, when, what it costs, what you do not do. Offer a true referral when you have one. A clear no to the wrong fit is a yes the right person can hear.

A second dialect from a brand exercise can blur the boundary further. If staff say "the pantry" and the site says "nourishment collective," people who were referred in plain speech will think they have the wrong organization. Use the plain speech. Voice is consistency. It is not a costume worn by the homepage and removed on the phone.

Hiding the shape of money is a related mistake. Free or not free. What a fee includes. What a suggested gift supports, without fake precision. A donate button with no shape asks the donor to guess and asks the participant to worry. Put the shape on the page. The people who will ask anyway should not have to.

## A shorter site you can keep true

After the cut, read what is left. A homepage with the work and a real door. Program blocks with outcome, boundary, and next step. A price and giving shape that matches intake. An about page with the people who currently run the work. A few proofs with decisions and consent. A report that opens. A contact path with short doors. If a page does not serve that set, give it a job or take it down.

Name an owner for the facts that rot. Hours, the open or full status, this year's report link, the staff names, the consent on photographs. Review them on the program's natural calendar. The site is a public record. Someone should tend it the way someone tends the room you invite people into.

Then look at the first screen on a phone, with the sad hero gone. The work should be obvious. The next step should be obvious. That is the repair.

Look at [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services) if you want a studio to make the cut and rebuild the pages that remain. Bring the current site and the program sentence you say at the door. Quiet and specific is the aim. Urgent and vague is the habit to leave behind.

The same discipline, pointed at a different buyer, starts with the homepage again. [What the homepage has to prove for a recruiting firm](/blog/what-the-homepage-has-to-prove-for-a-recruiting-firm) is the next piece, because a visitor who is judging a firm still needs one clear job from the first screen, and a different kind of proof than a program in the world.
